transcript: Header: 2026-08-12 15:00 UTC | Duration: ~62 mins | Attendees: Samir, Laura (Redwood); Maya, Ethan, Priya (BrightScale)

Summary: technical deep dive on throughput tuning — continuous batching, scheduler knobs, max_num_seqs, token limits, KV cache behavior, quantization tradeoffs, VPC constraints. Benchmarks and next steps at end.
Topics: continuous batching, batching window, scheduler 'max_num_seqs' and 'max_tokens', kv cache hit rates, quantization (4-bit/8-bit) perf, Dedicated vs Hosted on VPC, autoscale policies.
[00:00] Samir: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intros — Laura is our infra SE, she'll run through the tuning knobs. Maya, Ethan, Priya — thanks for making time.

[00:22] Maya: Thanks Samir. We're trying to push throughput on our chat endpoints. Current stack: self-hosted g4/p4 mixed right now with some spot evictions. Looking at Redwood for either Dedicated or private on-prem. Main ask: 10k requests/minute with p95 < 300ms for short responses (avg 60 tokens).

[00:45] Laura: Cool — if p95 300ms is the SLO, we need to tune batching to avoid latency amplification. We'll walk continuous batching, scheduler knobs like max_num_seqs and batching windows, and token limits. Also look at KV cache hit rate for chat workloads.
[01:10] Ethan: Quick note — our token distribution is pretty spiky. Most requests 20-80 tokens but a 2% tail that goes to 1200 tokens. That tail kills batching efficiency and causes memory pressure.
[01:38] Priya: Also, for BrightScale security team — VPC and KMS support is mandatory. Can you confirm Redwood Private supports customer KMS and does not exfil logs to public storage?
[01:56] Samir: Yes — Private supports customer-managed KMS/HSM and audit logs stay in your VPC when configured. We'll send the SOC2 and security pack. I'll add that to next steps.

[02:15] Laura: Starting with continuous batching — it's our low-latency mode that forms mini-batches on-the-fly. Key knobs: batching_window_ms (how long we wait), max_num_seqs (max sequences per batch), and max_total_tokens or token_limit to prevent OOM on long tails.
[02:45] Ethan: Is batching_window_ms adaptive or fixed? Our latency bucket is strict at p95.

[02:55] Laura: Can be adaptive. We recommend a small fixed window (5-10ms) for sub-300ms SLOs, and dynamic increase during spikes. Continuous batching uses micro-batches, so you get steady throughput without big tail latencies — tradeoff is slightly lower utilization vs huge batch windows.
[03:20] Maya: How does max_num_seqs interact with sequence length distribution? If we set it high, does it increase p99 due to long sequences forcing kernel flushes?

[03:38] Laura: Good q. max_num_seqs caps the number of concurrent sequences per batch. If sequences vary widely, it's safer to cap by tokens rather than seqs. Use max_total_tokens parameter — that limits the sum of tokens per batch and prevents long sequences from inflating GPU memory usage. We usually do a two-pass: set max_num_seqs=32 and max_total_tokens=4096 for 8k model tokens, then tune down if you see p95 regressions.
[04:10] Ethan: We saw earlier that increasing max_num_seqs improved throughput but latency p95 got worse during the tail. So use token cap — makes sense.

[04:25] Laura: Also remember KV cache behavior — for chat, prefix caching increases effective throughput by skipping computation for previous tokens. But cache size matters; cold starts still pay full cost. We monitor KV cache hit rate and adapt routing to warm caches for interactive users.
[04:50] Priya: Our on-prem environment has limited host memory. Any best practices for KV cache in constrained memory?

[05:02] Laura: Two levers: compressed KV (quantized keys) and cache eviction policy. Redwood has options to quantize cache entries (lossy) and to spill cold entries to disk. For memory-constrained boxes, use smaller cache size with higher hit-rate targeting active sessions only.
[05:28] Maya: Can you talk quantization tradeoffs? We heard 4-bit gives big perf gains but hurts QA for some prompts.

[05:37] Laura: Right — quantization (4-bit/8-bit) reduces memory and allows larger batch sizes or higher max_num_seqs. 4-bit int variants can regress on certain benchmarks; we recommend model-aware quant profiles. For throughput-first endpoints where output tolerance is higher, 4-bit may be acceptable. For sensitive LLM outputs, start with 8-bit or mixed precision and run regression evals.
[06:05] Ethan: Do quantized kernels change latency characteristics per token? I assume faster per-token, but decode may become memory bound?

[06:15] Laura: Generally faster due to reduced memory bandwidth, but kernel selection matters. Our runtime picks optimized kernels for quantized models; you'll often see ~1.6-2x throughput improvement depending on model and sequence length.

[06:40] Samir: Let's walk a sample tuning recipe for you given your token distribution: start with continuous batching, batching_window_ms=8, max_num_seqs=24, max_total_tokens=3072, enable prefix KV for active sessions, quantization=8-bit on non-sensitive routes. Then run a sweep: vary max_num_seqs 16/24/32 and token cap 2048/3072/4096 and watch p50/p95/p99.
[07:15] Maya: Sounds good. For scheduling, what scheduler knobs are available? We're using Kubernetes + custom autoscaler now.

[07:25] Laura: Scheduler knobs: per-worker concurrency, max inflight requests, batching_window_ms, queue_mode (fifo vs priority), and per-route routing weights. On Dedicated we expose these via route config. Also autoscale triggers: queue_length, GPU_util, and latency breach count.
[07:52] Ethan: If we set per-worker concurrency too high with long tail tokens, will it cause OOMs? We want a safe default.

[08:00] Laura: Yes — that's why token caps are safer. Default safe starting point: concurrency 4 per GPU, max_num_seqs 16, token cap 2048 for long models. Monitor OOMs and set 'reject_on_oom' to fail-fast and route to smaller model variant.
[08:25] Maya: Do you support automatic fallback to a smaller model variant during load?

[08:34] Samir: Yes — routing policies can fallback to cheaper variants or different regions. Redwood's smart routing can also route by cost/latency tiers. We'll show a config example in the follow-up.
[08:50] Priya: On the VPC/on-prem note — if we go Private, how are updates handled? We need staged rollouts and the ability to pin model versions.

[09:01] Laura: Private deployment has a control plane that you can run in your VPC; we support canary rollouts and pinning. For air-gapped, updates are packaged and you control upgrade windows. We'll share the ops runbook.
[09:20] Ethan: Benchmarks — do you have a standard harness? We want reproducible runs with our traces.

[09:28] Laura: Yes — we use a benchmark harness that replays user traces preserving token timing. Please share your traces; we'll run with same concurrency and token distribution. I've attached a sample config in the deck and we'll run the sweep with continuous batching and quantized models. Link to bench sheet: https://redwood.app/benchmarks/brightscale-2026 (note: internal link)
[09:55] Maya: On observability — we need token-level cost per route and per-user latency breakdowns for billing. Does Redwood provide that?
[10:06] Samir: Redwood Console gives token-level cost breakdowns, per-route dashboards, traces, and an export for billing. For Private you can push metrics to your Prometheus/Grafana.
[10:25] Priya: One of our constraints is encryption in transit and at rest — KMS integration details?
[10:33] Laura: We support customer-managed KMS for model encryption and you can bring your own keys. We'll include the KMS integration guide and sample policies in the follow-up.
[10:50] Ethan: Back to continuous batching — what does a micro-batch look like in practice? Are calls grouped by latency bucket or model shape?

[10:59] Laura: Grouping is by compatible shapes (sequence length) and model variant. We try to batch similar lengths together to minimize padding overhead. There's a small cost to grouping but it increases GPU utilization.
[11:20] Maya: If we have multi-tenant traffic, how do you prevent noisy neighbor effects in batching?

[11:30] Laura: Use per-tenant routing weights and isolation pools. Dedicated pools give isolation, and you can use priority queueing for latency-sensitive tenants. We can also pin critical routes to smaller models with lower concurrent batch sizes.
[11:50] Ethan: Performance numbers — any ballpark improvements from tweaking max_num_seqs?

[11:57] Laura: Empirically, increasing max_num_seqs from 8 -> 24 often yields ~2-3x throughput for short tokens before hitting memory or kernel limits. But p95 can increase if batch windows grow too long; that's why combining token caps and small windows is effective.
[12:20] Maya: Can we see telemetry from a previous customer that ran similar tuning?

[12:28] Samir: We can share anonymized traces and a case study — BrightScale-like occupant was HappyMetrics where continuous batching + 8-bit quant gave 2.1x throughput and kept p95 within SLO after tuning.
[12:45] Ethan: Any gotchas on GPU type? We have mixed A100 and T4. Which is recommended for throughput tuning?

[12:54] Laura: A100 gives better memory and throughput for long sequences and larger batches. T4 is cost-effective for short-token high-concurrency workloads but watch memory. Kernel choices differ; we'll recommend per-hardware kernel configs.
[13:15] Priya: About autoscaling — can we prioritize latency SLO over cost, i.e., scale aggressively on p95 breaches?
[13:23] Laura: Yes — autoscale policies can be configured to use latency breach counts to spin up capacity immediately. There's also burst capacity options for Dedicated to handle short spikes.
[13:40] Maya: We have a 2% tail of long requests — would you recommend routing tails to a background worker or throttling them?

[13:49] Laura: Tails are best handled by separate routes: route short interactive requests to low-latency pool with tight batch windows, and route long tail or batch jobs to a different pool where you can amortize cost with large batch windows and higher max_num_seqs.
[14:10] Ethan: On caching again — do you have metrics to show cache warm-up time and hit rates onto dashboards?
[14:19] Samir: Yes — Console shows KV cache hit rate, miss histogram, and per-route warm-up curves. We'll include what to monitor to identify cold-start impact.
[14:35] Maya: For our initial pilot, what's the minimum footprint to test throughput?
[14:41] Laura: For pilot: 2 GPU workers (A100 ideally), continuous batching with max_num_seqs=16, token cap 2048, and 8-bit quant. That'll give actionable numbers for your traces.
[15:00] Ethan: If we go Private, how long to provision a Dedicated-like environment?
[15:07] Samir: Dedicated reserved pools can be provisioned in a couple of weeks; Private deployment depends on networking and approvals — typically 4-8 weeks for VPC setup and KMS integration.
[15:25] Priya: Any licensing or legal concerns with quantized models or model weights on-prem?
[15:34] Samir: Licensing depends on model choice. We'll provide a checklist for model licensing and data residency. Private keeps weights in your environment.
[15:50] Maya: Let's talk concrete benchmark plan and success criteria. Our success criteria: throughput meets 10k req/min and p95 < 300ms for short-path. For long-path, p95 can be higher but < 2s.

[16:09] Laura: Plan: you share traces and p95 targets. We run three sweeps: baseline (no quant, conservative knobs), throughput-first (higher max_num_seqs, 8-bit), and latency-first (tight windows, lower num seqs). We'll deliver p50/p95/p99 and KV cache hit rates and utilization.
[16:35] Ethan: Good. What artifacts will you share?
[16:39] Laura: Benchmark spreadsheet, raw logs, recommended route config (JSON), and a short ops runbook for tuning knobs.
[16:52] Maya: Any immediate risks we should watch out for?
[16:57] Laura: Watch OOMs from tail tokens, noisy neighbors, and model regressions from aggressive quantization. We'll gate quantization behind regression evals on your eval set.
[17:15] Samir: I'll send the security pack and pricing. Laura will run the bench and share configs. Ethan will push traces. Anything else?
[17:25] Priya: Please include the KMS integration steps and a sample IAM policy for the control-plane agent.
[17:33] Samir: Noted — adding to action items.
[17:40] Closing recap: Next steps and owners reiterated: Laura runs bench (due 8/19), Ethan uploads traces (due 8/14), Samir sends pricing and security docs (due 8/16).
[17:55] Maya: Thanks all — excited to see the bench numbers.
[18:02] Samir: Thanks — we'll follow up with the sheet and schedule a bench review next week.
[62:00] Meeting end
